kurals.tamil:
அவாஎன்ப எல்லா உயிர்க்கும் எஞ்ஞான்றும்
தவாஅப் பிறப்பீனும் வித்து.
kurals.transliteration:
Avaa enba ellaa uyirkkum egnaandrum
Thavaaap pirappeenum viththu.
kurals.meaning: The wise say that desire is the seed which, for every living being and at every time, unfailingly produces birth after birth.
kurals.elementary: A seed falls into the ground and grows into a plant, and that plant drops more seeds that grow again and again. Valluvar says wanting things is like that seed: as long as we keep wanting, we keep getting planted into new lives, over and over.
kurals.university: The chapter that closes the ascetic section (Thuravaraviyal) opens by naming avaa (craving) as the vittu, the seed, of an unbroken chain of births (thavaap pirappu). The agricultural metaphor is exact: a seed holds the whole future plant, and craving holds the whole future of embodied existence, so destroying the seed leaves the cycle nothing to grow from. The word “enba” (“they say”) shows Valluvar reporting a consensus of the wise rather than inventing a doctrine, and the idea is indeed shared across Indian soteriologies: the Upanishadic teaching that desire determines rebirth, the Buddhist second noble truth that craving leads to renewed existence, and the Jain account of passions binding karma. Placed right after “Knowledge of Truth” (Meyyunarthal) and just before “Destiny” (Oozh), the chapter that ends Book 1, this chapter makes the uprooting of desire the practical summit of the renunciant’s path.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “He who forms desires in his mind, is born again through his desires here and there. But to him whose desires are fulfilled and who is conscious of the true Self (within himself) all desires vanish, even here on earth.”
hinduism.explanation: The Upanishad teaches that it is desire itself that pulls a person back into birth again and again, and that desire falls away only when the true Self is known.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts name desire as the thing that keeps producing new births. The verse just before it in the Mundaka even calls this the “seed” that the wise go beyond.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Near-exact doctrinal match: desire as the direct cause of rebirth. Mundaka 3.2.1 in the same passage even uses the image of a ‘seed’.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But every man is tempted, when he is drawn away of his own lust, and enticed. Then when lust hath conceived, it bringeth forth sin: and sin, when it is finished, bringeth forth death.”
christianity.explanation: James describes desire as something that conceives and gives birth: lust gives birth to sin, and sin grows up into death.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural’s ‘seed’, James treats desire as the thing everything else grows from. Here it produces sin and death, not rebirth.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong match on desire as the generative origin of a harmful chain; differs because Christianity has no rebirth cycle.

islam.quote_or_event: “And I do not acquit myself. Indeed, the soul is a persistent enjoiner of evil, except those upon which my Lord has mercy.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an describes the lower self (nafs) as constantly urging a person toward wrongdoing unless God’s mercy restrains it.
islam.tie_back: Both locate the root of trouble inside a person’s own urges. Islam sees the result as sin, not a cycle of rebirth.
islam._accuracy_note: Partial: identifies inner inclination (nafs/hawa) as the root of evil, but has no concept of rebirth.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Rabbi Elazar Ha-kappar said: envy, lust and [the desire for] honor put a man out of the world.”
judaism.explanation: The Mishnah names three forms of craving that drive a person out of a good life in this world and out of the world to come.
judaism.tie_back: Both treat desire as the root of a person’s ruin. The Kural says desire keeps producing births, while the Mishnah says it drives a person out of the world.
judaism.source: Pirkei Avot 4:21 (trans. Joshua Kulp, Mishnah Yomit)
judaism._accuracy_note: Thematic match on desire as destructive root; the mechanism (rebirth) is absent.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “The origin of suffering, as a noble truth, is this: It is the craving that produces renewal of being accompanied by enjoyment and lust, and enjoying this and that; in other words, craving for sensual desires, craving for being, craving for non-being.”
buddhism.explanation: In his first sermon, the Buddha teaches that craving (tanha) is what produces renewed existence, which is rebirth.
buddhism.tie_back: This is almost the same statement as the Kural: craving is the seed that keeps producing new births.
buddhism.source: Samyutta Nikaya 56.11, Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta (trans. Ñanamoli Thera)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Essentially one-to-one: the Second Noble Truth names craving as the cause of ‘renewal of being’ (ponobbhavika).

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Eros (Love), fairest among the deathless gods, who unnerves the limbs and overcomes the mind and wise counsels of all gods and all men within them.”
greek_mythology.explanation: In Hesiod’s creation story, Eros (Desire) is one of the very first powers to exist, and it drives all the later pairings and births of the gods.
greek_mythology.tie_back: In both texts desire comes first and generations grow out of it. Hesiod honors that power, while Valluvar wants it removed.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Next-best match: desire as the primordial generative force, but Greek myth celebrates rather than condemns it and has no rebirth doctrine.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Schopenhauer argues that the world is driven by a blind “will-to-live”, a restless striving. All willing springs from lack and so from suffering. Each satisfied wish only makes room for new ones, and the only real deliverance is for the will to deny itself.
philosophy.explanation: For Schopenhauer, endless wanting is the engine that keeps life and suffering going. Peace comes only when wanting itself is given up.
philosophy.tie_back: This is close to the Kural’s claim that desire is the seed of ceaseless existence. Schopenhauer himself pointed to Indian thought as a parallel.
philosophy.source: Arthur Schopenhauer, The World as Will and Representation, Vol. 1, §§ 56-57, 68 (paraphrase)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase, not a verbatim quote. Strong structural parallel, since Schopenhauer drew explicitly on Indian sources, but he gives a metaphysics of will rather than a literal rebirth doctrine.

kurals.tamil:
வேண்டுங்கால் வேண்டும் பிறவாமை மற்றது
வேண்டாமை வேண்ட வரும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Vendungaal vendum piravaamai matradhu
Vendaamai venda varum.
kurals.meaning: If you must desire something, desire freedom from rebirth. That freedom comes only when you desire to be free of desire.
kurals.elementary: Imagine you get just one wish. The smartest wish would be: “I wish I didn’t need any more wishes.” Valluvar says that is the one wish worth making, because it is the wish that sets you free.
kurals.university: The couplet repeats the verb vendu (“to want”) four times: vendungaal vendum … vendaamai venda. The verbal knot mirrors the paradox it describes. Valluvar admits that a person cannot simply switch off wanting, so he turns the power of desire against itself and makes piravaamai (non-birth, liberation) its one proper object. Parimelazhagar reads vendaamai as the settled state of desirelessness, so the means (wanting not to want) and the goal (not being born again) are joined. The same ‘desire for desirelessness’ paradox appears in the Buddhist distinction between wholesome aspiration (chanda) and craving (tanha), and in the Gita’s call to act without craving the fruits of action.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “No man can be made happy by wealth. Shall we possess wealth, when we see thee? Shall we live, as long as thou rulest? Only that boon (which I have chosen) is to be chosen by me.”
hinduism.explanation: Death offers the boy Nachiketas wealth, long life, kingdoms and pleasures. He refuses them all and insists on the one thing worth wanting: knowledge of what lies beyond death.
hinduism.tie_back: Nachiketas acts out the Kural’s advice. If you must want something, want the one thing that frees you from death and birth.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong narrative match: all lesser desires are rejected for the single desire for liberating knowledge.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Set your affection on things above, not on things on the earth.”
christianity.explanation: Paul tells believers to point their desires toward heavenly things rather than earthly ones.
christianity.tie_back: Both redirect desire instead of simply crushing it: if you must want, want the highest thing.
christianity._accuracy_note: Good match on redirecting desire; the object (heaven versus non-birth) differs.

islam.quote_or_event: “But you prefer the worldly life, While the Hereafter is better and more enduring.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an criticizes people for chasing the passing world instead of the lasting life to come.
islam.tie_back: Both urge that desire be spent only on what is final and lasting, not on what passes.
islam._accuracy_note: Moderate: redirects preference toward the enduring, but lacks the paradox of ‘desiring desirelessness’.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Whom have I in heaven but thee? and there is none upon earth that I desire beside thee.”
judaism.explanation: The psalmist says God is the only thing he truly desires, in heaven or on earth.
judaism.tie_back: Both narrow all wanting down to a single highest object. For the psalmist that object is God, and for Valluvar it is freedom from birth.
judaism._accuracy_note: Moderate: shares the ‘one desire only’ structure; the object differs.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Beset by craving, people run about like an entrapped hare. Therefore, one who yearns to be passion-free should destroy his own craving.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada speaks of a person who yearns to be free of passion and who reaches that goal by destroying craving.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the same paradox: a yearning for passionlessness is the one legitimate desire, and it works by ending desire.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Very close: the ‘yearning to be passion-free’ is fulfilled through destroying craving.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: As a young man, Heracles meets two women at a crossroads. Vice promises him an easy road of every pleasure. Virtue promises hard work that leads to true and lasting good, and Heracles chooses Virtue.
greek_mythology.explanation: The fable shows a hero turning down a life of gratified desires in favor of one higher goal.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural, it is about choosing what to want. The wise choice gives up the many pleasures for the one lasting good.
greek_mythology.source: Prodicus’ ‘Choice of Heracles’, in Xenophon, Memorabilia 2.1.21-34 (paraphrase)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Next-best match: a choice between pleasures and a higher good, but there is no idea of liberation from birth.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “But, for the present, totally suppress desire: for, if you desire any of the things which are not in your own control, you must necessarily be disappointed; and of those which are, and which it would be laudable to desire, nothing is yet in your possession.”
philosophy.explanation: Epictetus tells the beginner to set desire aside entirely. Wanting external things brings disappointment, and he is not yet able to want the right things properly.
philosophy.tie_back: Both treat suspending desire as the doorway to freedom. The only thing worth pursuing is the state that no longer craves.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Strong match on deliberate suppression of desire as the path; Stoic freedom is not framed as freedom from rebirth.

kurals.tamil:
வேண்டாமை அன்ன விழுச்செல்வம் ஈண்டில்லை
ஆண்டும் அஃதொப்பது இல்.
kurals.transliteration:
Vendaamai anna vizhuchchelvam eendillai
Aandum aqdhoppadhu il.
kurals.meaning: There is no treasure in this world as precious as freedom from desire. Even in the world beyond, nothing equals it.
kurals.elementary: A kid with a giant pile of toys who always wants more still feels poor. A kid who is happy with what they have feels rich. Valluvar says not wanting is the biggest treasure there is, bigger than anything here or even in heaven.
kurals.university: Vizhuchchelvam (“choicest wealth”) turns the idea of wealth inside out: a chapter on renunciation borrows the language of ownership to describe the absence of wanting. The pair eendu (“here”) and aandu (“there”) covers both this world and the heavenly worlds that ritual religion promised as rewards. Valluvar therefore ranks desirelessness above celestial pleasures, in line with the Upanishadic and Buddhist view that heaven is only a finer object of desire. The paradox that wanting less makes one richer shows up almost word for word in Seneca, in the Hadith on ‘richness of the soul’ and in Ben Zoma’s “Who is rich?”, which makes this one of the most cross-culturally shared couplets in the chapter.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “O Pārtha, when a man gives up all varieties of desire for sense gratification, which arise from mental concoction, and when his mind, thus purified, finds satisfaction in the self alone, then he is said to be in pure transcendental consciousness.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna describes the person of steady wisdom as one who has dropped all desires and is fully content within himself.
hinduism.tie_back: Both say that being content without desire is the real fullness. It needs nothing outside itself, which is the very definition of wealth.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong: desirelessness as self-sufficient contentment; the Gita does not use the ‘wealth’ metaphor explicitly.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But godliness with contentment is great gain.”
christianity.explanation: Paul tells Timothy that the real profit in life is godliness joined with contentment, not riches.
christianity.tie_back: Both reverse the usual idea of gain. Not wanting more is itself the greatest wealth.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong match on contentment as true ‘gain’.

islam.quote_or_event: “Wealth is not in having many possessions, but rather (true) wealth is feeling sufficiency in the soul.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet teaches that real richness is inner sufficiency (ghina al-nafs), not a large amount of property.
islam.tie_back: This is almost the Kural’s exact claim. The greatest wealth is a soul that no longer craves.
islam._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one: redefines wealth as the soul’s freedom from want.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Who is rich? He who rejoices in his lot”
judaism.explanation: Ben Zoma teaches that the truly rich person is the one who is content with what he has.
judaism.tie_back: Both redefine riches as freedom from wanting more.
judaism.source: Pirkei Avot 4:1 (trans. Joshua Kulp, Mishnah Yomit)
judaism._accuracy_note: Very close parallel; Avot speaks of contentment rather than complete desirelessness.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Health is the most precious gain and contentment the greatest wealth. A trustworthy person is the best kinsman, Nibbana the highest bliss.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha names contentment as the greatest wealth a person can have.
buddhism.tie_back: This is a direct parallel: the absence of craving is the supreme treasure.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Near-verbatim thematic match (‘contentment the greatest wealth’).

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Baucis and Philemon, a poor old couple, live contentedly in a humble cottage and gladly share what little they have with disguised gods. Their hut is turned into a temple, and they ask only to serve there and to die together.
greek_mythology.explanation: The couple’s happiness comes from contentment, not from possessions. Even when the gods reward them, they ask for almost nothing.
greek_mythology.tie_back: They live out the Kural’s idea that not wanting is the richest state. They are poor in goods but lack nothing.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Illustrative narrative of contented poverty; the ‘greatest wealth’ claim is implied rather than stated.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “It is not the man who has too little, but the man who craves more, that is poor.”
philosophy.explanation: Seneca argues that poverty is measured by craving, not by possessions.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the mirror image of the Kural: if craving is poverty, then being free of craving is the greatest wealth.
philosophy.source: Seneca, Moral Letters to Lucilius, Letter 2.6 (trans. R. M. Gummere)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one inversion of the Kural’s claim.

kurals.tamil:
தூஉய்மை என்பது அவாவின்மை மற்றது
வாஅய்மை வேண்ட வரும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Thoouymai enbadhu avaavinmai matradhu
Vaaaimai venda varum.
kurals.meaning: Purity is nothing other than freedom from desire, and that freedom comes from longing for truth.
kurals.elementary: A glass of water looks clear when nothing is stirring it up. Your heart is “clean” when wanting isn’t stirring it. The way to keep it calm is to love what is true more than what is shiny.
kurals.university: Valluvar defines thooymai (purity) psychologically rather than ritually, not by baths, diet or caste observances but as avaavinmai, the absence of craving. The second line adds a cause: freedom from craving arises from desiring vaaymai. Parimelazhagar and Mu. Varadarasan gloss vaaymai as meipporul, ultimate Reality, while Karunanidhi reads it as truthfulness. Either way the chapter keeps its strategy of redirecting desire, letting one longing, for truth, push out all lesser ones. The lengthened forms thoouymai and vaaaymai (alapedai, a metrical lengthening) bind the two key terms by sound as well as sense.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “As fire is covered by smoke, as a mirror is covered by dust, or as the embryo is covered by the womb, the living entity is similarly covered by different degrees of this lust.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna compares desire to smoke over a fire or dust on a mirror, something that clouds the soul’s natural clarity.
hinduism.tie_back: Both treat purity as what remains when desire is removed. Take away the dust of craving and the mirror is clean.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong on desire as the defilement of purity; the Kural’s second line (truth as the means) is less directly mirrored.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Seeing ye have purified your souls in obeying the truth through the Spirit unto unfeigned love of the brethren, see that ye love one another with a pure heart fervently:”
christianity.explanation: Peter tells believers that their souls have been purified by obeying the truth.
christianity.tie_back: This matches the Kural’s causal chain very closely: purity comes by way of truth.
christianity._accuracy_note: Close structural match (truth → purified soul); does not define purity specifically as desirelessness.

islam.quote_or_event: “He has succeeded who purifies it, And he has failed who instills it [with corruption].”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an says success belongs to the one who purifies the soul (tazkiyat al-nafs) of its base inclinations.
islam.tie_back: Both make purity an inner cleansing of the self, not an outward ritual.
islam._accuracy_note: Moderate: inner purification of the soul; the link to truth is not explicit.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Who shall ascend into the hill of the LORD? or who shall stand in his holy place? He that hath clean hands, and a pure heart; who hath not lifted up his soul unto vanity, nor sworn deceitfully.”
judaism.explanation: The psalm defines the pure person as one who has not set his soul on empty things and has not sworn falsely.
judaism.tie_back: Both tie purity to not craving empty things and to truthfulness, which are the two halves of the Kural.
judaism._accuracy_note: Good match: purity is linked both to not desiring ‘vanity’ and to truthfulness.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “‘All conditioned things are impermanent’ — when one sees this with wisdom, one turns away from suffering. This is the path to purification.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada teaches that seeing the truth about impermanence makes a person turn away from craving, and that this is purification.
buddhism.tie_back: This has the same logic as the Kural: seeing truth leads to the end of craving, and that is purity.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Strong structural match: truth (insight) → turning from craving → purification.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Socrates’ myth of the winged soul, souls follow the gods to gaze on true Being in the ‘plain of truth’, and their wings are nourished by it. Souls weighed down by base appetite lose their wings and fall.
greek_mythology.explanation: The soul stays pure and winged by feeding on truth, and it falls when appetite drags it down.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural, it links a pure soul to longing for truth and a fallen soul to craving.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Philosophical myth rather than traditional mythology; parallel is thematic.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the Phaedo, Socrates describes philosophy as a “purification” (katharsis). The lover of wisdom separates the soul from bodily pleasures and desires, which ‘nail’ the soul to the body, so that it can grasp truth itself.
philosophy.explanation: For Plato, purity means freedom from bodily cravings, and it comes through the love of wisdom and truth.
philosophy.tie_back: This is almost the Kural’s formula: purity is freedom from desire, and it is reached by desiring truth.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase. Strong parallel on both halves of the couplet.

kurals.tamil:
அற்றவர் என்பார் அவாஅற்றார் மற்றையார்
அற்றாக அற்றது இலர்.
kurals.transliteration:
Atravar enbaar avaaatraar matraiyaar
Atraaga atradhu ilar.
kurals.meaning: Only those who have cut off desire deserve the name of true renunciants. Others, whatever they have given up, are not free in the same complete way.
kurals.elementary: Throwing your candy away doesn’t really count if you keep thinking about candy all day. Valluvar says the real “giver-upper” is the person who stopped wanting, not just the person who stopped having.
kurals.university: The couplet plays on atravar (“those who are cut off”, the renunciants) and avaa atraar (“those cut off from desire”), and ends by saying that others are not free in that full sense (atraaga atradhu ilar). Valluvar draws a sharp line between outward renunciation (robes, poverty, leaving home, the themes of the earlier chapter Thuravu) and inward renunciation. This extends his critique of the false ascetic in Chapter 28 (Koodaavozhukkam, “Imposture”). For Valluvar, freedom is measured by what one no longer wants, not by what one no longer owns.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “A person who has given up all desires for sense gratification, who lives free from desires, who has given up all sense of proprietorship and is devoid of false ego – he alone can attain real peace.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna says that only the one who has given up desires inwardly, not just outwardly, reaches real peace.
hinduism.tie_back: The Gita’s “he alone” matches the Kural’s claim that only the desire-free are truly renunciants.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Very close: exclusive claim (‘he alone’) tied to inner desirelessness.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And they that are Christ’s have crucified the flesh with the affections and lusts.”
christianity.explanation: Paul defines true belonging to Christ as having put to death the desires themselves, not just outward behavior.
christianity.tie_back: Both locate true renunciation in the death of inner desire.
christianity._accuracy_note: Good match on inner renunciation as the defining mark; lacks the explicit contrast with merely outward renouncers.

islam.quote_or_event: “Be in this world as if you were a stranger or a traveler.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet tells Ibn ‘Umar to hold the world loosely, like a traveler passing through who doesn’t cling to anything.
islam.tie_back: Both describe detachment as an inner stance toward the world. The hadith does not spell out the Kural’s contrast between inner and outer renunciation.
islam._accuracy_note: Partial: inner detachment is implied, but the inner-versus-outer contrast is not stated.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Who is mighty? He who subdues his [evil] inclination”
judaism.explanation: Ben Zoma teaches that real strength is mastering one’s own desires (the yetzer), not conquering others.
judaism.tie_back: Both redefine an honored title (the ‘mighty’, the ‘renunciant’) so that it belongs to whoever has mastered inner desire.
judaism.source: Pirkei Avot 4:1 (trans. Joshua Kulp, Mishnah Yomit)
judaism._accuracy_note: Structural parallel (redefining a title by inner mastery); speaks of subduing, not eliminating, desire.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “There is one who, turning away from desire (for household life) takes to the life of the forest (i.e., of a monk). But after being freed from the household, he runs back to it. Behold that man! Though freed, he runs back to that very bondage!”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha describes a man who outwardly renounces home life but, with his craving still intact, runs straight back to it.
buddhism.tie_back: This is exactly the Kural’s point: outward renunciation without cutting off craving is not true freedom.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Very close: the failed outward renunciant who has not cut off craving.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: After washing away his golden touch, King Midas comes to hate riches and goes to live in the woods and fields as a worshipper of Pan. But his foolish mind stays unchanged, and he soon earns a pair of ass’s ears for judging Pan’s music above Apollo’s.
greek_mythology.explanation: Midas outwardly gives up wealth, but he has not been inwardly transformed.
greek_mythology.tie_back: He loosely illustrates the Kural’s warning that outward renunciation is not the same as true inner freedom.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Weak/next-best: Midas’ flaw is folly rather than lingering desire; used as the closest mythic image of incomplete renunciation.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Whoever, then, would be free, let him wish nothing, let him decline nothing, which depends on others else he must necessarily be a slave.”
philosophy.explanation: Epictetus defines freedom as wanting nothing that depends on things outside oneself. Anyone who still wants such things remains a slave.
philosophy.tie_back: This is a direct parallel. Only the one who has cut off desire is truly free, and everyone else is still bound.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one: freedom is defined exclusively by the absence of desire.

kurals.tamil:
அஞ்சுவ தோரும் அறனே ஒருவனை
வஞ்சிப்ப தோரும் அவா.
kurals.transliteration:
Anjuva dhoorum arane oruvanai
Vanjippa dhoorum avaa.
kurals.meaning: To stand in fear of desire is itself virtue, because it is desire that deceives and ruins a person.
kurals.elementary: Some joke toys look like candy but have a spring inside that jumps out at you, so you learn to be careful of them. Valluvar says wanting things is a trick like that. It fools us, so being careful of it is part of being good.
kurals.university: The couplet frames the ethical life as vigilance: aran (virtue) here simply is the fearing (anjuvadhu) of avaa, because avaa is what vanjippadhu, what cheats and betrays a person. Commentators such as Mu. Varadarasan add that desire waits for a moment of weakness (sorvu) to strike, much as a thief waits for the watchman to nod off. The repeated expletive oorum gives the line a proverbial, almost incantatory rhythm. This picture of desire as a cunning inner enemy parallels the Gita’s portrait of kama as an “all-devouring” foe and the biblical image of sin crouching at the door.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “It is lust only, Arjuna, which is born of contact with the material mode of passion and later transformed into wrath, and which is the all-devouring sinful enemy of this world.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna names desire (kama) as the great enemy that drives people into wrongdoing even against their will.
hinduism.tie_back: Both portray desire as an inner enemy to be feared and guarded against.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong: desire as the enemy; the element of deception is implied (Gita 3.40 speaks of it deluding the embodied).

christianity.quote_or_event: “That ye put off concerning the former conversation the old man, which is corrupt according to the deceitful lusts;”
christianity.explanation: Paul describes lusts as “deceitful”: they promise good but corrupt the person who follows them.
christianity.tie_back: This matches the Kural’s key claim that desire is the thing that deceives.
christianity._accuracy_note: Very close on ‘deceitful’ desire; the call to fear is implied in ‘put off’.

islam.quote_or_event: “But as for he who feared the position of his Lord and prevented the soul from [unlawful] inclination, Then indeed, Paradise will be [his] refuge.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an praises the one who, out of fear of God, holds the soul back from its desires (hawa).
islam.tie_back: Both join fear and the restraint of desire as the heart of righteousness.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong: fear + restraining desire = the righteous path; the object of fear is God rather than desire itself.

judaism.quote_or_event: “If thou doest well, shalt thou not be accepted? and if thou doest not well, sin lieth at the door. And unto thee shall be his desire, and thou shalt rule over him.”
judaism.explanation: God warns Cain that sin crouches at the door like a predator waiting for its chance, and that he must master it.
judaism.tie_back: Both picture a lurking inner force waiting to ambush a person, and both urge vigilance against it.
judaism._accuracy_note: Good image-level match (lurking, predatory inner force); ‘sin’ rather than desire per se, though rabbinic tradition links it to the yetzer hara.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Those who are lust-infatuated fall back into the swirling current (of samsara) like a spider on its self-spun web. This, too, the wise cut off. Without any longing, they abandon all suffering and renounce the world.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha compares people trapped by lust to a spider caught in the web it spun itself.
buddhism.tie_back: Both show desire as a self-made trap that fools its victim, which is why the wise watch out for it.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Good match on desire as a self-deceiving trap.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Warned by Circe that the Sirens’ sweet song lures sailors to their death, Odysseus stops his crew’s ears with wax and has himself tied to the mast. When he begs to be set free, his men only tie him tighter.
greek_mythology.explanation: Odysseus knows the song of desire will fool him, so he fears it wisely and guards himself ahead of time.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the Kural in story form: fear desire, because it deceives even the wise.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Excellent narrative parallel for vigilant fear of deceptive desire.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Human infirmity in moderating and checking the emotions I name bondage: for, when a man is a prey to his emotions, he is not his own master, but lies at the mercy of fortune: so much so, that he is often compelled, while seeing that which is better for him, to follow that which is worse.”
philosophy.explanation: Spinoza calls the power of passions over us “bondage”. They mislead us into following the worse even when we can see the better.
philosophy.tie_back: Both describe desire as something that tricks a person against their own good, which is why it must be guarded against.
philosophy.source: Spinoza, Ethics, Part IV, Preface (trans. R. H. M. Elwes)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Strong on desire misleading the self; Spinoza speaks of emotions generally and prescribes understanding rather than fear.

kurals.tamil:
அவாவினை ஆற்ற அறுப்பின் தவாவினை
தான்வேண்டு மாற்றான் வரும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Avaavinai aatra aruppin thavaavinai
Thaan vendum aatraan varum.
kurals.meaning: If a person cuts off desire completely, the deeds that lead to an undying life will come to him just as he wishes.
kurals.elementary: When you stop grabbing at every toy in the store, your hands are finally free to hold what really matters. Valluvar says that when you drop all your wants, good deeds that last forever come to you easily.
kurals.university: Aatra aruppin, “if one cuts utterly”, insists on total rather than partial removal and echoes the chapter title’s aruththal (“cutting”). Thavaa vinai, “unfailing” or “imperishable action”, is glossed by commentators as the deeds that bring deathlessness, that is, liberation. The promise that these deeds arrive thaan vendum aatraan (“in the way he wishes”) holds a quiet irony: the person who has stopped wanting finally gets what he wants. The same paradox, that giving up self-will lines the will up with the good, appears in Stoic acceptance of fate, in the rabbinic “do His will as though it were your will”, and in the Katha Upanishad’s promise that the desireless mortal becomes immortal.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “When all desires that dwell in his heart cease, then the mortal becomes immortal, and obtains Brahman.”
hinduism.explanation: Death teaches Nachiketas that the complete ending of all desires is what makes a mortal immortal.
hinduism.tie_back: Both promise that cutting off desire completely yields what does not perish.
hinduism.source: Katha Upanishad 2.3.14 (numbered II.6.14 in trans. Max Müller, SBE 15)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one: total cessation of desire → immortality.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And the world passeth away, and the lust thereof: but he that doeth the will of God abideth for ever.”
christianity.explanation: John contrasts the passing world and its desires with the one who does God’s will and so lasts forever.
christianity.tie_back: In both, leaving desire behind leads to deeds and a life that endure forever.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong: transient desire versus enduring deeds/life.

islam.quote_or_event: “Wealth and children are [but] adornment of the worldly life. But the enduring good deeds are better to your Lord for reward and better for [one’s] hope.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an sets the fleeting objects of worldly desire against “the enduring good deeds” (al-baqiyat al-salihat).
islam.tie_back: The Qur’an’s “enduring good deeds” closely echo the Kural’s thavaa vinai, the deeds that do not perish.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong verbal parallel (‘enduring deeds’ ≈ ‘unfailing deeds’); the conditional on cutting desire is implicit.

judaism.quote_or_event: “He used to say: do His will as though it were your will, so that He will do your will as though it were His. Set aside your will in the face of His will, so that he may set aside the will of others for the sake of your will.”
judaism.explanation: Rabban Gamaliel teaches that the one who sets aside his own will finds his will fulfilled.
judaism.tie_back: This is the same paradox as the Kural: give up your wants, and what is good comes “as you wish”.
judaism.source: Pirkei Avot 2:4 (trans. Joshua Kulp, Mishnah Yomit)
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong structural match on the ‘surrender your will, receive your will’ paradox.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Let go of the past, let go of the future, let go of the present, and cross over to the farther shore of existence. With mind wholly liberated, you shall come no more to birth and death.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha urges total letting go, which brings the deathless state beyond birth and death.
buddhism.tie_back: Both promise that complete relinquishment leads to the undying.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Good: complete letting go → deathlessness; the ‘as one wishes’ element is absent.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Achilles reveals that his mother foretold two fates for him: a long but inglorious life at home, or death at Troy with glory that will never perish (kleos aphthiton).
greek_mythology.explanation: Achilles weighs the comforts of a long life against deeds whose fame will not die.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is a loose echo of the Kural’s thavaa vinai, “imperishable deeds”. Achilles, however, trades comfort for glory, which is itself a desire.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Weak/next-best: shares the idea of ‘imperishable deeds’, but Achilles’ motive is desire for fame, which the Kural would reject.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Don’t demand that things happen as you wish, but wish that they happen as they do happen, and you will go on well.”
philosophy.explanation: Epictetus teaches that when you give up demanding outcomes, things turn out “well”, because your will now matches reality.
philosophy.tie_back: This mirrors the Kural’s paradox: cut off desire, and things come as you wish.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Strong on the paradox of surrendered wishing; no notion of immortality.

kurals.tamil:
அவாஇல்லார்க் கில்லாகுந் துன்பம் அஃதுண்டேல்
தவாஅது மேன்மேல் வரும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Avaa illaarkku illaagum thunbam aqdhundel
Thavaaadhu menmel varum.
kurals.meaning: Those without desire have no sorrow. Where desire exists, sorrow comes without fail, one after another.
kurals.elementary: Every time you want something you can’t have, you feel a little sad. If you want a hundred things, you get a hundred little sads. Want nothing, and the sads have nowhere to come from.
kurals.university: The couplet is a strict pair of conditions. For those without desire (avaa illaarkku), suffering ceases to exist (illaagum); if desire exists (aqdhundel), suffering comes thavaaadhu menmel, without fail, one upon another. The doubled menmel (“more and more, upon and upon”) imitates the way craving compounds, since each satisfied desire breeds new ones. This is the Kural’s closest approach to a formal statement of the Buddhist second noble truth, but Valluvar stays practical rather than metaphysical: he describes the lived economy of wanting, not a theory of dependent origination.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “While contemplating the objects of the senses, a person develops attachment for them, and from such attachment lust develops, and from lust anger arises. From anger, complete delusion arises, and from delusion bewilderment of memory. When memory is bewildered, intelligence is lost, and when intelligence is lost one falls down again into the material pool.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna traces a chain reaction: attachment breeds desire, desire breeds anger, and each stage brings a further downfall.
hinduism.tie_back: Both show desire setting off an unending cascade of suffering, each trouble bringing the next.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong: desire as the start of a compounding chain of ruin.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But they that will be rich fall into temptation and a snare, and into many foolish and hurtful lusts, which drown men in destruction and perdition. For the love of money is the root of all evil: which while some coveted after, they have erred from the faith, and pierced themselves through with many sorrows.”
christianity.explanation: Paul warns that craving riches leads into snares and “many sorrows”.
christianity.tie_back: This matches the Kural closely: where desire is, sorrows pile up.
christianity._accuracy_note: Very close: craving → ‘many sorrows’; focused on wealth rather than desire in general.

islam.quote_or_event: “So as for he who transgressed And preferred the life of the world, Then indeed, Hellfire will be [his] refuge.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an warns that the one who prefers worldly desires ends in suffering.
islam.tie_back: Both link giving in to worldly desire with inevitable suffering. The Qur’an places that suffering in the hereafter, the Kural in this life.
islam._accuracy_note: Partial: desire for the world → suffering, but eschatological rather than the Kural’s immediate psychology.

judaism.quote_or_event: “He that is greedy of gain troubleth his own house; but he that hateth gifts shall live.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs warns that greed brings trouble on one’s own household, while the one who rejects bribes will live.
judaism.tie_back: Both say that desire itself produces trouble and that freedom from it brings life.
judaism._accuracy_note: Moderate: greed → trouble; narrower than the Kural’s claim about all desire.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Just as a tree, though cut down, sprouts up again if its roots remain uncut and firm, even so, until the craving that lies dormant is rooted out, suffering springs up again and again.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches that as long as the root of craving remains, suffering keeps growing back.
buddhism.tie_back: This is almost identical to the Kural: where craving remains, suffering comes “again and again” (menmel).
buddhism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one, including the ‘again and again’ recurrence.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the underworld, Tantalus stands in a pool beneath fruit-laden trees. Whenever he stoops to drink the water drains away, and whenever he reaches for fruit the wind whirls the branches out of reach, so his torment never ends.
greek_mythology.explanation: Tantalus suffers forever because his desire is endless and never satisfied.
greek_mythology.tie_back: He embodies the second half of the Kural: where desire remains, suffering keeps coming without end.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Strong image of desire-driven endless suffering; in myth it is a punishment rather than a natural consequence.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Socrates tells a parable in which the craving part of a foolish soul is like a leaky jar or sieve. It must be filled again and again and is never satisfied, so its owner lives in constant distress, unlike the orderly person whose jars are sound and full.
philosophy.explanation: Plato argues that a life of ever-renewed desire is a life of ceaseless labor and pain.
philosophy.tie_back: This mirrors the Kural’s claim that where desire exists, suffering keeps coming, while the desire-free are at rest.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase. Strong parallel on desire as the source of unending toil.

kurals.tamil:
இன்பம் இடையறா தீண்டும் அவாவென்னும்
துன்பத்துள் துன்பங் கெடின்.
kurals.transliteration:
Inbam idaiyaraa theendum avaavennum
Thunbaththul thunbam kedin.
kurals.meaning: When desire, the worst of all sorrows, is destroyed, joy flows without a break, even in this life.
kurals.elementary: Imagine an itch you’ve had for so long that you forgot it was there. When it finally stops, you feel wonderful all the time. Valluvar says wanting is that itch, and when it’s gone, happiness just keeps going.
kurals.university: Valluvar calls avaa “thunbaththul thunbam”, the sorrow among sorrows, the one that gives rise to all the others. Removing it therefore does more than take away one pain: it dries up the source of every pain. The promised result, inbam idaiyaraadhu eendum, is unbroken joy “even here” (eendum), a this-worldly liberation comparable to the Upanishadic jivanmukta and to the Buddhist realization of nibbana in this very life. The joy is defined negatively, as what remains when craving stops. That lines up closely with the Buddhist third noble truth and with Epicurus’s definition of pleasure as freedom from disturbance.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “A person who is not disturbed by the incessant flow of desires – that enter like rivers into the ocean, which is ever being filled but is always still – can alone achieve peace, and not the man who strives to satisfy such desires.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna compares the desire-free sage to the ocean: rivers pour in, but it stays full and still, at lasting peace.
hinduism.tie_back: Both promise an unbroken inner peace once craving no longer stirs a person.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong: the end of craving → steady, unbroken peace.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Not that I speak in respect of want: for I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content.”
christianity.explanation: Paul describes a steady contentment that no change of circumstance can break.
christianity.tie_back: Both describe a lasting happiness that no longer depends on getting what one wants.
christianity._accuracy_note: Good: unconditional contentment; does not name desire as ‘the sorrow of sorrows’.

islam.quote_or_event: “O reassured soul, Return to your Lord, well-pleased and pleasing [to Him],”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an speaks of the soul at rest (al-nafs al-mutma’innah), the opposite of the restless, evil-urging self.
islam.tie_back: Both describe a settled joy that follows once the restless self is calmed.
islam._accuracy_note: Moderate: the tranquil soul is the goal; its link to ending desire is implicit in the nafs doctrine.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Surely I have behaved and quieted myself, as a child that is weaned of his mother: my soul is even as a weaned child.”
judaism.explanation: The psalmist compares his quieted soul to a weaned child that no longer craves its mother’s milk and rests content.
judaism.tie_back: Both picture a soul weaned from craving that finds calm, lasting peace.
judaism._accuracy_note: Good image of peace born of being ‘weaned’ from craving.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Cessation of suffering, as a noble truth, is this: It is remainderless fading and ceasing, giving up, relinquishing, letting go and rejecting, of that same craving.”
buddhism.explanation: The Third Noble Truth teaches that suffering ends when craving ends completely.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the most central possible match: when craving, the source of suffering, is destroyed, what remains is lasting peace.
buddhism.source: Samyutta Nikaya 56.11, Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta (trans. Ñanamoli Thera)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one: the cessation of craving is the cessation of suffering (nirodha).

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Hesiod tells of a race of heroes whom Zeus settled after death in the Islands of the Blessed at the ends of the earth. They live there untouched by sorrow while the fertile land bears fruit for them.
greek_mythology.explanation: Greek myth imagines a state of unbroken happiness free from sorrow.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is a distant parallel to the Kural’s unbroken joy. In the myth it is a reward granted by the gods, not the result of ending desire.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Weak/next-best: shares the image of sorrowless bliss but not its cause (the end of desire).

philosophy.quote_or_event: “By pleasure we mean the absence of pain in the body and of trouble in the soul.”
philosophy.explanation: Epicurus defines the highest pleasure as tranquility (ataraxia), which is reached by cutting away needless desires.
philosophy.tie_back: Both define the highest joy negatively, as what remains when the disturbance of desire is gone.
philosophy.source: Epicurus, Letter to Menoeceus 131 (trans. R. D. Hicks)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Strong: joy as the absence of disturbance; Epicurus prunes vain desires rather than eliminating all desire.

kurals.tamil:
ஆரா இயற்கை அவாநீப்பின் அந்நிலையே
பேரா இயற்கை தரும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Aaraa iyarkai avaa neeppin annilaiye
Peraa iyarkai tharum.
kurals.meaning: Desire by nature can never be satisfied. Whoever casts it off gains, in that very moment, a nature that never changes: lasting bliss.
kurals.elementary: Trying to fill a bucket that has a hole in the bottom never works. You pour and pour, and it’s never full. Valluvar says wanting is that leaky bucket. Stop pouring into it, and you find a calm that never runs out.
kurals.university: The final couplet crowns the chapter with a mirrored wordplay: aaraa iyarkai (a nature that is never filled) against peraa iyarkai (a nature that never departs). Insatiability is what defines desire, and permanence is the reward for giving it up, the unchanging state that commentators identify with liberation (veedu). The word annilaiye (“in that very state” or “at that very moment”) suggests the reward is not postponed to some later heaven but is the same thing as the act of letting go. As the last couplet on renunciation before the chapter on Destiny that closes the Book of Virtue, it sums up Valluvar’s whole ascetic path: the endlessly hungry becomes the endlessly at peace.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Thus the wise living entity’s pure consciousness becomes covered by his eternal enemy in the form of lust, which is never satisfied and which burns like fire.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna describes desire (kama) as duspura, “never to be satisfied”, a fire that only grows the more it is fed.
hinduism.tie_back: The Gita’s “never satisfied” matches the Kural’s aaraa iyarkai, the nature that is never filled.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Very close on insatiability; the Gita here does not state the reward of permanence.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Jesus answered and said unto her, Whosoever drinketh of this water shall thirst again: But whosoever drinketh of the water that I shall give him shall never thirst; but the water that I shall give him shall be in him a well of water springing up into everlasting life.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus contrasts water that leaves people thirsty again with “living water” that ends thirst forever.
christianity.tie_back: Both contrast an endless thirst with an everlasting, unchanging fullness.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong structural match (insatiable thirst → permanent satisfaction); the means is grace rather than relinquishment.

islam.quote_or_event: “If Adam’s son had a valley full of gold, he would like to have two valleys, for nothing fills his mouth except dust. And Allah forgives him who repents to Him.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet teaches that human greed is bottomless and only death (“dust”) finally fills it.
islam.tie_back: This is a direct parallel to the Kural’s aaraa iyarkai: desire is by nature never full.
islam._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one on the insatiability of desire.

judaism.quote_or_event: “He that loveth silver shall not be satisfied with silver; nor he that loveth abundance with increase: this is also vanity.”
judaism.explanation: Kohelet observes that the lover of wealth is never satisfied, however much he gains.
judaism.tie_back: Both identify never being satisfied as the defining nature of desire.
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong on insatiability; does not state the reward of permanence.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “There is no satisfying sensual desires, even with the rain of gold coins. For sensual pleasures give little satisfaction and much pain. Having understood this, the wise man finds no delight even in heavenly pleasures. The disciple of the Supreme Buddha delights in the destruction of craving.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches that even a rain of gold cannot satisfy desire, and that the wise delight in the destruction of craving.
buddhism.tie_back: This matches both halves of the Kural: desire is insatiable, and joy lies in ending it.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one on both insatiability and the delight of its destruction.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Erysichthon cuts down Ceres’ sacred oak and is punished with Famine. The more he eats, the hungrier he becomes. He spends his wealth, sells his daughter, and finally devours his own body.
greek_mythology.explanation: His curse is an appetite that can never be filled and only grows as it is fed.
greek_mythology.tie_back: He is a mythic picture of the Kural’s aaraa iyarkai, the nature that is never satisfied.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Excellent image of insatiable desire; the myth has no ‘permanent bliss’ counterpart.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “The wealth required by nature is limited and is easy to procure; but the wealth required by vain ideals extends to infinity.”
philosophy.explanation: Epicurus distinguishes natural needs, which have limits, from vain desires, which have no limit and can never be satisfied.
philosophy.tie_back: Both identify limitless, insatiable desire as the problem, and both locate peace in stepping out of it.
philosophy.source: Epicurus, Principal Doctrines 15 (trans. R. D. Hicks)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Strong on insatiability of vain desire; Epicurus keeps natural desires rather than removing all desire.
